lines.text: Forest tribes, emperors and reformers, two world wars, a divided capital and a nation made whole again. This is the story of Germany.
In the year nine, Germanic tribes led by Arminius ambushed three Roman legions in the northern forests. Rome never pushed far beyond the Rhine again.
Centuries later Charlemagne, king of the Franks, conquered much of western and central Europe, and in the year 800 the Pope crowned him emperor.
From Otto the First, an elected emperor held the German lands loosely together in the Holy Roman Empire, a patchwork that lasted some eight hundred years.
Around 1450, in Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg printed with movable metal type. Cheap books soon carried new ideas across Europe.
Martin Luther, a monk and professor, challenged the Church over the sale of indulgences, and translated the Bible into German.
His protest grew into the Reformation, which split Western Christianity into Catholic and Protestant, and brought wars of religion.
It started in 1517 with his Ninety-five Theses. Spread in print, a university debate became a movement.
In the north-east, the duchy of Prussia began its long rise, toward a kingdom famed for its army and its civil service.
Johannes Kepler showed that the planets move in ellipses, not circles, laying down laws that Newton would later explain.
Then came the Thirty Years' War. Begun over religion, it became a European struggle for power, and some German regions lost a large share of their people.
From the recovering land came Johann Sebastian Bach, organist and composer of the Brandenburg Concertos and the Mass in B minor.
Frederick the Great seized Silesia, held it against much of Europe, played the flute, and made Prussia a great power.
In Konigsberg, Immanuel Kant argued that the mind shapes how we experience the world, and that moral duty follows from reason.
Goethe wrote Faust and Young Werther, studied plants and colour, and served at the court of Weimar.
Beethoven wrote nine symphonies and kept composing after he went deaf, carrying music from the Classical to the Romantic.
In 1791 the Brandenburg Gate rose in Berlin, crowned by a chariot of victory. It would one day stand for a whole divided nation.
The brothers Grimm gathered folk tales like Hansel and Gretel, and their collection became one of the most translated German books.
Otto von Bismarck, the Prussian statesman, would lead three short wars and bring the German states together as one empire.
Karl Marx argued that history is driven by struggles between classes. With Engels he wrote the Communist Manifesto, which shaped politics worldwide.
The doctor Robert Koch proved that specific germs cause specific diseases, finding the bacteria of tuberculosis and cholera.
Friedrich Nietzsche questioned morality and religion, declared that God is dead, and urged people to create their own values.
Karl Benz patented a practical petrol car in 1886, and his wife Bertha drove it a long way to prove it worked.
Rudolf Diesel designed an engine that ignites its fuel by squeezing air, more efficient than the petrol engines of his day.
Max Planck showed that light and heat come in tiny packets of energy, and quantum theory was born.
Wilhelm the Second, the last German emperor, would dismiss Bismarck, build a great navy, and lead Germany into the First World War.
Through wars with Denmark, Austria and France, Bismarck and Prussia drew the German states together.
In 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, soon an industrial and military power.
For the first time, Germany stood as one country at the centre of Europe. Today it has the largest economy in the European Union.
Konrad Adenauer, born that decade, would one day be West Germany's first chancellor, tying it to the West and making peace with France.
Albert Einstein, born in Ulm, would transform physics with relativity and win a Nobel Prize.
Adolf Hitler, born in Austria, would lead the Nazi Party to power, start the Second World War and carry out the Holocaust.
Marlene Dietrich became a star in The Blue Angel, went to Hollywood, and spoke out against the Nazi regime.
In 1914 Germany went to war. Four years later millions were dead, four empires had fallen, and Europe's map was redrawn.
From defeat came the Weimar Republic, a democracy beset by violence and crisis, even as Berlin flourished in art, film and science.
In Weimar, Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus, whose plain forms for industry shaped modern architecture and design.
The Treaty of Versailles made Germany give up land, shrink its army and accept blame for the war, a bitter peace.
By 1923 money was almost worthless, people carried banknotes in wheelbarrows, and savings were wiped out.
In 1933 Hitler took power, and Germany became a one-party dictatorship under the Nazis.
On a November night in 1938, synagogues and Jewish shops were smashed and burned, Jews were killed, and thousands of men arrested.
In 1939 Germany invaded Poland, beginning the largest war in history.
Under cover of war, Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered about six million European Jews, as well as Roma, disabled people and others.
In the spring of 1945 the Red Army surrounded Berlin. Hitler killed himself, and Germany surrendered days later.
At Nuremberg, Allied judges tried leading Nazis for war crimes, and laid the ground for international criminal law.
In 1948 the Soviets cut the routes to West Berlin, and the Western Allies fed the city by air for almost a year.
In 1949 West Germany adopted its Basic Law, written to guard against dictatorship, opening with the protection of human dignity.
That same year, in the Soviet zone, the communist German Democratic Republic was founded. The nation was split in two.
In the east, in 1954, Angela Merkel was born. A physicist, she would become Germany's first woman chancellor.
A year later came Friedrich Merz, the Christian Democrat who would become chancellor in 2025.
And Olaf Scholz, the Social Democrat who would lead Germany through war in Ukraine and an energy crisis.
In 1961 East Germany built a wall straight through Berlin, to stop its people leaving.
Then everything changed. On the third of October 1990, East Germany joined the Federal Republic, and Germany was one again.
It began on the ninth of November 1989, when the border opened and crowds poured through and broke down the Wall.
Reunited Germany helped launch the euro, and in 2002 the German mark gave way to the new notes and coins.
In 2006 Germany hosted the World Cup, remembered for its festive mood across the country.
Soon after, a worldwide banking crisis struck, and governments spent huge sums to rescue failing banks.
In Brazil in 2014, Germany beat the hosts seven to one, then Argentina in the final, to win the World Cup.
In 2015, more than a million people reached Europe, many fleeing war in Syria, and Merkel's Germany took in the most.
In 2022 Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and Germany faced war in Europe once more.
From the forests of Arminius to a reunited Berlin, Germany's long story is still being written.
